title_ar: شرح ورقات إمام الحرمين في أصول الفقه -الشريط الرابع
title_en: Commentary on the Waraqāt of Imam al-Haramayn on legal theory — tape four
body_ar:
النسخ:

عقد هذا الباب لبيان النسخ و ذكر أقسامه، و النسخ معناه في اللغة الإزالة، فيقال نسخت الرياح الأثر إذا أزالته و غيرته و يقال نسخت الشمس الظل إذا أزالته، و يطلق أيضا على النقل فيقال نسخ الكتاب إذا نقله، فهذا معناه في اللغة.

و أما معناه في الاصطلاح فهو تغيير الحكم الشرعي بخطاب متراج عنه، و المقصود بالحكم الشرعي ما كان خطابا أيضا، فلا تنسخ البراءة الأصلية و لا ينسخ بها لأن الأحكام كلها إنما نزلت على براءة أصلية سابقة لها، فلو اعتبر ذالك نسخا لكانت الأحكام كلها ناسخة لأمر قد سبق و هو البراءة الأصلية و عدم التكليف و لا ينسخ أيضا إلا بالخطاب فلا نسخ بالقياس و لا بالاجتهاد و لا بالإجماع، و إنما يحصل النسخ بالوحي المنزل.

،قال وأما النسخ فمعناه لغة الإزالة يقال نسخت الشمس الظل إذا أزالته ، وقيل معناه النقل ، من قولهم نسخت ما في هذا الكتاب أي نقلته ..
body_en:
Abrogation:

This chapter is set out to explain abrogation and to mention its divisions. Naskh: its meaning in the language is removal. One says "the winds nasakhat the trace" when they removed it and altered it, and one says "the sun nasakhat the shade" when it removed it. It is also applied to transferring, so one says "he nasakha the book" when he copied it. This is its meaning in the language.

As for its meaning as a technical term, it is the alteration of a ruling of the Sharia by an address subsequent to it. What is meant by the ruling of the Sharia is one that was itself also an address — so the original absence of legal liability (al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah) is not abrogated, and nothing is abrogated by it, because all the rulings came down upon an original absence of liability that preceded them; and if that were reckoned to be abrogation, all the rulings would be abrogating something that had preceded, namely the original absence of liability and the absence of legal responsibility. Nor is anything abrogated except by an address: so there is no abrogation by analogical reasoning, nor by independent legal reasoning, nor by scholarly consensus; abrogation comes about only by revelation sent down.

, He said: "As for abrogation, its meaning in the language is removal. One says: the sun nasakhat the shade, when it removed it. And it is said that its meaning is transferring, from their saying: I nasakhtu what is in this book, that is, I copied it"..

options: by an address subsequent to it [reading mutarākhin ʿanhu]
by an address that supersedes it
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT, and the word carries the definition. Mutarāj is not a word in this construction. The definition of naskh in this literature turns on the abrogating address being LATER than the abrogated ruling — the standard formulation uses tarākhī, 'being subsequent, coming after an interval', and mutarākhin ʿanhu is almost certainly what was said. The point is not decorative: if the abrogating address were simultaneous with the abrogated one there would be a contradiction rather than an abrogation, which is precisely why the interval is in the definition. Translated on the reading mutarākhin, with the printed form preserved in body_ar and the departure recorded here rather than made silently.

options: preserve the order as served and flag it
move the quotation of the base text above the commentary
delete the final paragraph as a duplicate
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT, STRUCTURAL. The paragraph is the quotation of al-Juwayni's own words on naskh, which in a commentary is stated BEFORE the explanation, not after it. Here the Sheikh's explanation is given first and the text being explained appears last, introduced by a stray comma before qāla ('he said'). The paragraph also repeats, in shorter form, the two lexical senses already given above. This looks like a transcription or assembly error rather than anything the Sheikh did. The order is preserved and flagged; option 1 would silently restructure the record and option 2 would delete source text.

flags.context: the state that precedes all rulings and is said not to be subject to abrogation
options: the original absence of legal liability (al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah)
flags.note: Al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah is the state in which a person is under no obligation before a ruling addresses him; it underlies the presumption of continuity (istiṣḥāb) in the glossary. Option 1 must be avoided: 'innocence' imports the criminal-law sense and an English reader will hear the presumption of innocence, which is a different doctrine altogether. The term is not in the glossary and should be added.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on al-Waraqāt of Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni, a short primer on legal theory. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 649–652 and the tape numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the tape number in the title, not by id, and tape two does not appear anywhere in the range 601–652.

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text breaks off and the full material is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.

The Arabic verb nasakha has been kept in the three illustrative sentences on its lexical meaning, because the point being made is about that one word's range and replacing it with three different English verbs would destroy the point. The same device is used at id 644 for waqafa.

'Address' renders khiṭāb, God's addressing of His creatures through revelation. A ruling of the Sharia is an address in this sense, which is why the Sheikh can argue that only an address can abrogate one.
The three excluded means of abrogation are rendered by the glossary's fixed terms: analogical reasoning (qiyās), independent legal reasoning (ijtihād), scholarly consensus (ijmāʿ).
The record opens with a bare heading and no doxology, so the beginning of the lecture is not published.
